title: Why read him anyway
hookLine: a flawed man who wrote the most human Stoic letters

lines: A RICH MAN WHO PRAISED POVERTY.
cards: After the last two days, a fair question. Why have we spent sixty-some lessons with this man? A rich man who praised poverty.
An adviser who stayed close to a murderer. We could have spent the whole season with Epictetus, a former slave who owned almost nothing, or Marcus Aurelius, who at least ran the empire himself.
And yet readers have kept coming back to Seneca, and not in spite of his flaws exactly. Partly because of them.

teach.b: First, he admits things. Seneca tells Lucilius he got seasick and jumped overboard. That he wept too much for a friend.
That he's not wise. Epictetus teaches from the front of the room; Seneca writes from the next seat over, struggling with the same lesson. Second, he lived where most of us live.
Not in a cave, not on a throne.

teach.h: HE LIVED IN THE MIDDLE, LIKE US.
teach.b: In the middle: money, family, a job that asked things of him he didn't like. His letters are written from inside compromise, a place readers can recognize. Third, readers in every age.
Some early Christian readers warmed to him, and a set of letters between Seneca and the apostle Paul was forged and copied for centuries. The Christian writer Tertullian called him often one of ours.
Much later, the French essayist Montaigne named Seneca and Plutarch as the writers he drew on most. People from very different paths found a friend in him. Fourth, how he died.
Ordered by Nero to end his life, Seneca turned to his friends.
Tacitus says he told them that since he couldn't leave them gifts, he would leave the one thing he had, and the finest: the image of his life.
Paulina tried to die with him; Nero's soldiers saved her, and she lived on for some years. An image with stains on it. That may be exactly why it teaches.
A perfect man would be easy to admire and hard to learn from.

how: Some readers of Seneca keep a favorite letter or line to reread over the years, and read him alongside the honest record of his life rather than as a flawless sage.

o: the image of a life, left to friends at the end
a portrait painted to hang in the Senate
a written list of a person's debts and loans

games.q: why read him anyway — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca and the apostle Paul really wrote to each other
the letters were forged later, though widely read for centuries.
she tried to die with him; Nero's soldiers saved her and she lived some years more.
readers love Seneca because he seemed perfect
much of his pull is that he admits his faults and lived in the middle.

games.q: you're Seneca, ordered to die, with friends around you and nothing you're allowed to give them. what do you leave?
games.why: Tacitus says he left them the one thing he had, and the finest: the image of his life.

practice: Of all Seneca's lines in these sixty-some days, hold every hour, who is poor, the dark is in me, one sound rises, rich in enough, let one rise without forcing it, and ask what in your life it touched.
Picture him at his desk, an imperfect man writing for a friend, and yourself, also imperfect, reading it.

wordCard.voice: Imago vitae. Latin for the image of a life: what Tacitus says Seneca left his friends, admitting his faults, stains and all. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'the image of a life': what Tacitus says Seneca left his friends.

carryVoice: Your line: flawed and wise. The stains are part of the image he left. Until tomorrow.
